title: Albumin + Furosemide (Push/Pull)
sources: Critical Vector — Push/Pull: Albumin & Furosemide (physiology deep dive + content audit)
Lee TH et al. Albumin + furosemide meta-analysis. PLOS One 2021 (13 studies, 422 pts)
Chalikias G et al. Furosemide ± albumin in ADHF with hepatic dysfunction (RCT). Am Heart J 2026
Itagaki Y et al. Albumin + diuretic in ventilated hypoalbuminemic patients (meta-analysis). 2022
Levick JR, Michel CC. Microvascular fluid exchange and the revised Starling principle. Cardiovasc Res 2010

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV push/pull deep dive. When it works, which bottle, dose, timing, and when it's a waste.

summary: A rescue for the congested, diuretic-resistant, hypoalbuminaemic patient — NOT a license to over-resuscitate and clean up later. It works by turning down capillary filtration (raised plasma oncotic pressure) while the lymphatics keep draining — not by 'sucking' fluid back. Effect is modest, real, and concentrated in a narrow population.

items: Serum albumin < 2.5 g/dL — the subgroup that shows benefit in every positive meta-analysis.
ADHF with hepatic dysfunction, or significant cardiorenal congestion (the population of the 2026 Chalikias RCT).
Diuretic resistance after maxing the loop dose and adding a thiazide.
Ventilated hypoalbuminaemic patient where improving the P/F ratio is the immediate target (Itagaki 2022: ~3× more likely to improve oxygenation, fewer hypotensive episodes — no mortality benefit).

Active sepsis with brisk capillary leak — proteases shred the glycocalyx, albumin crosses into the interstitium, the oncotic gradient collapses, and infused albumin largely becomes expensive interstitial fluid.
Albumin > 2.5 g/dL — minimal pharmacokinetic payoff; the 'albumin as a ride for protein-bound furosemide' argument only applies at the low end (< 2 g/dL).
Under-dosing (< 30 g total albumin) — below where the meta-analytic benefit appeared.
Nephrotic syndrome — infused albumin is substantially lost in the urine.
As a substitute for treating why the patient is congested.

rows: 25% (hyperoncotic) — this is the push/pull bottle (100 mL expands plasma volume ~350–500 mL by recruiting interstitial fluid). Save 5% for cirrhosis indications (large-volume paracentesis, SBP prophylaxis, HRS) — 5% here is filling the bathtub when the goal is draining it.

Give the furosemide within 30–60 min of the albumin. Albumin plasma half-life is only 6–10 h (faster in critical illness) — the urine-output effect is significant at ~8 h and gone by 24 h. Unlinked orders hours apart miss the window.
Max the loop first (and add a thiazide) — push/pull is added on top of a maxed regimen, not instead of it.
Urine output over the first 12 h, sodium, creatinine, and for pulmonary/venous congestion. Effect is filtration-limited — expect a slow drain, not a bolus diuresis.

body.text: Mechanism (why the old 'suction' pitch is wrong)

items: Revised Starling (Levick & Michel 2010): there is no meaningful venous oncotic 'suck-back' — filtration dominates along the whole capillary. The lymphatics, not the veins, return filtered fluid.
The glycocalyx is the real semipermeable barrier; the oncotic gradient that matters is plasma vs the thin protein-free subglycocalyx space, not plasma vs the bulk interstitium.

25% albumin raises plasma oncotic pressure → less fluid filters out; the lymphatics keep draining at their existing rate → the swollen tissue slowly dries out. Turn down the faucet while the drain keeps running.

In heart failure, high central venous pressure raises the pressure the thoracic duct empties against — a lymphatic-outflow problem layered on top of raised filtration, not purely a 'low albumin' problem.

Lee 2021 meta-analysis (13 studies, 422 pts): albumin + furosemide beat furosemide alone by +31 mL/hr urine and +1.8 mEq/hr sodium — effect concentrated where albumin < 2.5 g/dL, cumulative furosemide > 30 g, renal impairment present, measured within 12 h.

Chalikias 2026 (RCT, ADHF + hepatic dysfunction, n = 241): furosemide + albumin — better symptom relief (P < .001), less worsening renal function (25% vs 38%), smaller creatinine rise (0.07 vs 0.18 mg/dL), ~1 day shorter stay.
MIMIC-IV septic-hypoalbuminaemia cohort: lower in-hospital mortality with albumin + loop diuretic (25.5% vs 36.5%) — hypothesis-generating observational data, not proof.

body.text: Prevention beats rescue: resuscitate only patients who are both fluid-responsive AND fluid-tolerant, and reach for pressors/inotropes when the heart says yes but the venous system says no (VExUS-guided). That produces fewer congested, intravascularly-dry patients who later need this maneuver.

buildNote: Tier 3. A VExUS / venous-congestion assessment module is the natural companion (referenced in the closing callout and in septic-shock-resuscitation).
